questions.question: What is the central lookup and placement invariant in HBase?
options: Every qualifier must exist in every row
The row key determines sort order, region ownership, and the primary lookup path
Every table has exactly one region
All rows are joined by HBase before a read returns
questions.explanation: HBase orders rows lexicographically by row key and partitions contiguous key ranges into regions. That one key therefore controls both locality and load distribution.

questions.question: Why does a timestamp-first row key usually create a write hotspot?
options: Timestamps cannot be compared as bytes
New monotonically increasing keys keep landing in the final key-range region
The WAL accepts only one timestamp per second
Bloom filters reject recent values
questions.explanation: Monotonic prefixes concentrate all current appends at one end of the sorted table, so one RegionServer receives most of the write load.

questions.question: What trade-off does salting a time-series row key introduce?
options: It removes durability from writes
It spreads writes but requires range reads to fan out across salt buckets
It forces all columns into one family
It disables region splitting
questions.explanation: A salt prefix distributes adjacent timestamps among key ranges. A time-window query must issue one bounded scan per salt bucket and merge the results.

questions.question: When may a client treat an HBase write as durable under the normal contract?
options: After the mutation is appended to the WAL according to the configured sync policy and applied to MemStore
Only after the next major compaction
As soon as a client creates a Put object
After every replica scans the row
questions.explanation: MemStore is volatile. The WAL is the replay source that protects an acknowledged mutation until its data is flushed into durable HFiles.

questions.question: Which atomicity guarantee is native to HBase?
options: Serializable transactions across arbitrary tables
Atomic mutations scoped to one row
Atomic range scans across every region
Atomic major compaction across a cluster
questions.explanation: HBase provides strongly consistent row operations and atomic mutation within one row. Workflows spanning unrelated rows require an application-level design.

questions.question: Daily logical growth is 1,200 GiB and the target region size is 12 GiB. About how many region splits per day does the simple planning model predict?
questions.explanation: The rough split rate is daily growth divided by target region size: 1,200 / 12 = 100. Real split timing also depends on key distribution and existing region sizes.

questions.question: What happens when sustained compaction rewrite demand exceeds available compaction bandwidth?
options: The backlog grows, increasing store-file count, read amplification, and eventually write stalls
HBase automatically changes every row key
The WAL no longer needs replication
Reads become relational joins
questions.explanation: Compaction debt accumulates immutable files. Reads inspect more files, disk space is reclaimed later, and flush or write pressure can eventually stall foreground traffic.

questions.question: A RegionServer fails after acknowledging WAL-protected writes that were not yet flushed. What is the safe recovery path?
options: Discard its WAL because MemStore was not flushed
Reassign its regions and replay the surviving WAL edits before normal service resumes
Run a full-table scan from every client
Promote ZooKeeper to store the table data
questions.explanation: The master coordinates reassignment while WAL edits reconstruct accepted mutations that had not reached HFiles. HDFS supplies the durable files and WAL storage.
